places.name: Alesund

visits.text: Ålesund's city centre is a unique case in Europe: on the night of 23 January 1904, a fire razed 850 houses in 16 hours and left 10,000 people homeless. The entire town was rebuilt in brick and concrete between 1904 and 1907 in the then-fashionable Art Nouveau style – hence this rare architectural coherence. Stroll along Kongens gate and St Olav square to see the turrets, ornate façades, and floral motifs.

The Jugendstilsenteret is housed in the former Svaneapoteket pharmacy from 1907, whose original interior has been preserved. The museum traces the 1904 fire, the accelerated reconstruction, and the Art Nouveau influences from Germany – Kaiser Wilhelm II, who regularly holidayed in Sunnmøre, had sent four relief ships after the disaster.

Ålesund's harbour and its quays facing the Sunnmøre Alps give the quintessential view of the town from the water. Walk to the end of Molovegen to see the old wooden warehouses - some converted into cafés - and the red lighthouse at the harbour entrance.

The Sunnmøre Museum, in Ålesund's Borgundgavlen district, displays historic houses and traditional boats that illustrate life on the coast. Explore the buildings of the open-air museum, then the exhibitions devoted to navigation and fishing to discover Sunnmøre's maritime heritage.

Atlanterhavsparken, on the Tueneset coast in Ålesund, presents the marine life of the Norwegian coast in its aquariums. Observe the cold-water fish, then head outside to the outdoor pools to see the seals and penguins.

activities.text: Climb the 418 steps to the Aksla viewpoint in Byparken park. The view over Ålesund and its islands, with the Sunnmøre Alps as backdrop, is the finest in town. The step numbers are printed on the risers if you need to keep count.

Walk along the Tueneset coast in Ålesund, near Atlanterhavsparken. Follow the coastal paths to see the rocks, small coves, and islands at the entrance to the fjord. Stop in the designated areas to watch the sea and the boats passing offshore, then return along the same path.

visits.text: Hjemmeluft is the main area open to visitors within the Rock Art of Alta, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985. More than 6,000 carvings have been recorded in the Alta region, including around 3,000 at Hjemmeluft. Created over several millennia, they depict moose, reindeer, boats and hunting scenes among other subjects. Walkways allow visitors to explore the carvings while protecting the site.

The Alta Museum, located on the rock carving site since 1991, presents carving techniques, the life of Arctic hunter-gatherers, and the northern lights—the first permanent aurora observatory was built in Alta in the late 19th century.

Alta's Nordlyskatedralen (Northern Lights Cathedral), inaugurated in 2013, stands out for its titanium spiral rising toward the sky. It evokes an aurora frozen in architecture—the visit is brief but the exterior is worth the detour.

The Alta River is one of the world's most coveted salmon rivers—Atlantic salmon regularly exceed 25 kg here, and fishing rights for non-residents reach the equivalent of 30,000 NOK for three days. Each year, a lottery allocates 70 fishing days to visiting anglers from among 1,200 applicants. Even without a fishing rod, walking along the banks under the midnight sun is breathtaking.

The Sami Siida, just outside Alta, is a traditional Sami camp where you can feed reindeer, listen to stories around the fire, and taste bidos—Sami reindeer stew—in a real lavvu. It's one of the most accessible Sami cultural experiences from Alta.

In Alta, discover Sami and Kven cultures in the exhibitions at Alta Museum, on the Hjemmeluft site. The objects and stories on display introduce the region's traditions, activities and history. Explore the galleries devoted to local communities to understand how these cultures meet in Finnmark.

The return to Alta through Finnmark's interior takes you through landscapes of tundra, rivers, and dwarf birch forests—the vast, inhabited emptiness at the end of the world. In autumn, the ochre and golden colors of the tundra are spectacular.

activities.text: Sautso Canyon, on the Alta River, is the deepest canyon in Northern Europe, with walls reaching 400 m in height over a length of 22 km. Boat excursions let you travel alongside its cliffs - check local departures from Alta.

In winter, go dog sledding on Finnmarksvidda - Norway's largest plateau stretches as far as the eye can see. Local sled dog kennels offer 2 to 3-hour outings with their huskies. In summer, guided hikes with the dogs are also organised.

Alta is one of the world's northern lights capitals in winter—the surrounding countryside, far from city lights, offers a perfectly dark sky. The best nights are from September to March, between 6pm and 2am.

The Alta River is renowned for world-class salmon fishing—local guides organize outings on the water in summer, fly-fishing or spinning. In summer, you can also rent a canoe to paddle along the riverbanks at your own pace.

visits.text: Gudbrandsjuvet, along the National Scenic Route, is a narrow gorge with steel walkways suspended above waterfalls. Allow for a round trip during the day from Åndalsnes. Stop for 20 minutes - the viewpoint architecture is exemplary, and the site empties out quickly.

Trollstigen - literally “the Troll Ladder” - climbs through 11 hairpin bends on a 9% gradient to an elevation of 858 meters, with the Stigfossen waterfall (a 320 m drop) right beside the road. Opened on July 31, 1936, by King Haakon VII after 8 years of construction by hand, each bend bears the name of the foreman who built it. Allow for a round trip during the day from Åndalsnes.

From the panoramic platform at the top of Trollstigen, designed by Reiulf Ramstad Architects, you look down at the hairpin bends and see the Isterdalen valley opening toward the Atlantic. Allow for a round trip during the day from Åndalsnes. Allow 30 minutes up there - the visitor center's café is worth a stop.

Åndalsnes, Norway's mountaineering capital, nestles at the head of the Romsdalsfjord beneath Romsdalshorn (1,550 m). It is an ideal base for hikers - the Norsk Tindesenter on the harbor houses the mountaineering museum and an indoor climbing wall.

Trollveggen is Europe's highest vertical rock face - 1,100 metres of gneiss from the valley floor to the summit, with a 50-metre overhang at the top. You can see it from the E136, 10 km from Åndalsnes. The first ascents didn't happen until 1965 - a British amateur team, mocked by experts, had taken up the challenge.

Trollveggen visitor centre, at the foot of the wall on the E136, offers a panoramic terrace and a film on the history of climbing attempts and BASE jumping - banned since 1986 after several fatal accidents.

activities.text: Driving the Geiranger-Trollstigen tourist route (around 104 km). Trollstigen is closed from November to mid-May depending on snow conditions – check vegvesen.no before departure. Vehicles over 12.4 metres are prohibited.

Hike to Rampestreken from Åndalsnes – a cantilevered steel platform 550 metres above Romsdalsfjord. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes for the 4 km round trip. The ascent is steep but the trail is marked. The view over the valley and fjords is worth every metre of elevation gain.

visits.text: On the E16 between Gudvangen and Voss, the road crosses the spectacular Nærøydalen valley, enclosed by steep mountainsides and dotted with numerous waterfalls. The old Stalheimskleiva road, famous for its 13 very tight hairpin bends, bears witness to the former route through this impressive terrain. Take your time to enjoy the views over the valley before continuing towards Voss.

Upon arrival in Bergen, stroll the Hanseatic wharf of Bryggen, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. In 1360, the Hanseatic League established its trading office here and controlled the dried fish trade for nearly 400 years - Bergen is the only non-League city whose original medieval structure still stands within the urban fabric. The current appearance dates from the reconstruction after the 1702 fire; 62 buildings survive.

Explore the alleys and warehouses behind the waterfront of Bryggen - the facade along the wharf is what everyone photographs, but the back of the rows of houses is far more interesting. You'll find craft galleries, jewellers' and potters' workshops set in spaces that haven't changed since the 18th century. In high season, arrive before 9am to have the alleys to yourself.

Fisketorget fish market is one of Norway's oldest open-air markets. You'll find fresh salmon, langoustines and halibut - plus stalls selling prepared dishes. The adjacent indoor market, open year-round, is the best option outside summer.

The Nordnes peninsula, at the western tip of Bergen's centre, offers a pleasant walk along the shore with views over Byfjord. The coastal park of Nordnesparken at the point is where Bergen locals come to swim in summer - the water is cold but the setting is beautiful.

Fantoft Stave Church, in Paradis south of Bergen, is a reconstruction. The original, a 12th-century stave church moved from Fortun in 1883, burned down in an arson attack in 1992. The identical reconstruction was completed in 1997. Visit the exterior and grounds - the carved doors with intertwined dragon motifs are particularly detailed.

The Milde Arboretum, in southern Bergen, is one of Norway's largest botanical gardens, with 50 hectares of rhododendron, conifer and coastal plant collections. The paths follow coves and mossy woodland - this is quiet Bergen, away from the tourist crowds, approximately 23 km from Bergen city centre, a 30-minute drive.

activities.text: Drive from Flåm to Bergen via the E16: allow 3 hours, including photo stops in the Nærøydalen valley. The section between Gudvangen and Voss is the most spectacular - do not rush through it.

Take the Fløibanen funicular from the city centre up to Mount Fløyen (320 m) - in service since 1918, 850 metres of track, 6 minutes uphill. The panoramic view over Bergen, its seven mountains and Byfjord is the city's essential postcard shot. At the summit, marked trails lead into the troll forest - allow 30 to 45 minutes for the loop around Lake Skomakerdiket. Book online to skip the queue in summer.

Walk through Milde's coastal woodland and rocky coves - the paths around the arboretum extend for several kilometres towards the fjord. The terrain is easy, ideal for a morning's walk in Norwegian nature without straying far from Bergen. From Bergen, allow approximately 23 km and a 30-minute drive to reach Milde.

visits.text: The fast crossing from Svolvær (or Skutvik) to Bodø across the Vestfjorden is by passenger-only express boat. If you are travelling with a car, arrange its transport separately: it cannot be taken aboard this service. Settle on the upper deck if the weather allows: the view of the Lofoten Islands receding to the north is spectacular. Bodø is 33 km north of the Arctic Circle.

Bodø's waterfront was completely rebuilt after the Second World War bombings in May 1940, which destroyed 75% of the town. Today, the harbour looks out towards the offshore islands and the mountains of Salten. It is a lively town and a departure point for ferries to the Lofoten Islands.

The Norwegian Aviation Museum (Norsk Luftfartsmuseum) opened in 1994—the building itself, seen from the air, traces the shape of an airplane propeller over 10,000 m². Inside, you'll encounter civilian and military aircraft from World War II to the present day, including a replica of the American U2 spy plane shot down in 1960 as it headed toward Bodø from Pakistan. Don't miss the flight simulator.

Moskenes→Bodø ferry: booking in advance is essential in summer—without a reservation, the wait can exceed 6 hours at the Moskenes dock. The crossing across Vestfjord takes 3 hours 15 minutes to 3 hours 45 minutes and can be choppy. It's also on this route that you can spot sea eagles and, in season, whales.

From Bodø, head to Saltstraumen 30 km southeast. In this 150-meter-wide strait, 400 million cubic meters of water rush through every 6 hours when the tide reverses, reaching 22 knots (40 km/h) and forming whirlpools 10 meters in diameter and 5 meters deep. It's officially the world's strongest tidal current, a phenomenon 2,000 to 3,000 years old. The spectacle is even more intense two to three days before or after the full and new moon—check tide times before going.

activities.text: The Saltstraumen, 33 km from Bodø, is the world's strongest tidal current: every 6 hours, 400 million cubic meters of water flow through a 150-meter-wide strait at speeds up to 20 knots (37 km/h), creating whirlpools 10 meters in diameter. Check schedules online before heading out—the phenomenon is invisible at slack tide. The effect is strongest on the days of the full and new moons.

If you have energy, climb Mount Keiservarden from Bodø for a panoramic view over the city, the sea and the silhouettes of the Lofoten on the horizon. That evening in Bodø is also the time to arrange the next leg: the flight to Tromsø the following morning.

visits.text: The Jæren Scenic Route follows 70 km of flat, windswept coastline—a geographical curiosity in Norway, land of mountains. Wild sandy beaches, dunes, and lighthouses unfold along this route protected since 1977.

Obrestad lighthouse (Obrestad fyr), built from solid granite in 1873, is the first land-based lighthouse on the Jæren coast. In its basement, German soldiers left frescoes during the occupation - these are accessible to visitors. Plan this as a day trip by car from Egersund.
Painted wooden houses line the harbor in Egersund's historic town center—a preserved maritime atmosphere and a few waterfront cafes. Allow 45 minutes to explore at leisure.

activities.text: The beaches of Bore and Orrestranden are among Norway's most beautiful: Orrestranden stretches over 3 km of white sand, while Borestranden is the go-to surf spot in Jæren. Wind, waves and an unobstructed horizon over the North Sea - a complete change of scenery. Plan this as a day trip by car from Egersund.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: Leaving Oslo on the E16, stop at Sundvollen for views over Tyrifjorden - one of Norway's largest lakes, nestled between conifer forests and hills. Continue on the E16 towards Fagernes and Lærdal, through valleys, forests and mountain landscapes dotted with red wooden farm buildings.

On the E16 between Lærdal and Aurland, you enter the Lærdal Tunnel - 24.5 km long, making it the world's longest road tunnel, opened in 2000. To break the monotony, engineers carved out three large caverns lit in blue and yellow at regular intervals. Don't speed: the limit is 80 km/h.

If the road is open, you can replace the drive through the Lærdal Tunnel with the scenic Aurlandsfjellet road (FV243), which crosses the mountains between Lærdal and Aurland. It offers high-mountain scenery and spectacular views down over the Aurlandsfjord. Allow more time than for the tunnel route. The section crossing the mountain plateau is closed in winter.

The Flåmsbana Museum, with free admission beside the station, traces the 20 years of construction of the Flåm Railway (1923–1940). The 20 km line descends 866 metres between Myrdal and Flåm, with a maximum gradient of 5.5% - one of the steepest in the world for standard gauge. 18 of the 20 tunnels were dug by hand by teams of 120 to 220 workers.

Otternes Bygdetun is a historic farm hamlet overlooking the Aurlandsfjord, about 4 km from Flåm. Its collection of wooden buildings reflects several centuries of traditional farming life in the region. The site can be reached by car or on foot from Flåm along the fjord. From the hamlet's meadows, there are beautiful views over the Aurlandsfjord and surrounding mountains.

Aurlandsvangen, the main village of the municipality of Aurland, 7 km from Flåm, has a peaceful waterfront on the Aurlandsfjord. Stop here in the late afternoon to see the evening light on the fjord's calm waters.

From the electric boat, the walls of the Nærøyfjord rise to 1,800 metres - and the fjord is only 250 metres wide at its narrowest point. The fjord has been UNESCO-listed since 2005: you will pass farms accessible only by boat. Book your tickets ahead in summer - the boats sail full.

Gudvangen, at the terminus of Nærøyfjord, is a village of a few dozen inhabitants squeezed between vertiginous cliffs. Its name means 'field of the gods at the water's edge' in Old Norse. Stop to see Kjelfossen waterfall, which plunges more than 800 metres from the heights.

activities.text: Drive from Oslo to Flåm via the E16. The road is passable all year round, but winter conditions can occur from November to April. Check vegvesen.no for road conditions before setting off.

Hike or photo walk along Flåm harbour and the shore of Aurlandsfjord. The village is tiny - a few hundred inhabitants - but the setting between fjord and sheer mountains is arresting. In high season, dozens of cruise ships anchor in the bay: arrive early in the morning for peace and quiet.

Silent cruise by electric boat on Nærøyfjord between Flåm and Gudvangen - 2 hours one way. The boat “Future of the Fjords”, fully electric since 2018, glides soundlessly between the fjord walls. The absence of an internal combustion engine is striking: you hear only waterfalls and the cries of eagles. Several departures daily, year-round.

visits.text: Flydalsjuvet viewpoint, accessible by car from Geiranger, offers the postcard view with the fjord below and the tiny village of Geiranger in the distance. This is where most aerial photos of the fjord are taken – go early in the morning to avoid the coaches.

Ørnesvingen (the Eagle's Bend), on the tourist route descending towards Geiranger, offers a direct panorama of the Seven Sisters and the fjord from the clifftop. On clear days, you can see the green water 600 metres below.

The Norwegian Fjord Centre (Norsk Fjordsenter) traces the history of inhabitants who lived on the farms overlooking Geirangerfjord. The fjord has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005 - both for its landscapes and for the traces of agricultural life in extreme conditions.

Dalsnibba (1,476 m) is Europe's highest viewpoint above a fjord accessible by car, about half an hour's drive from Geiranger. The toll road winds up from Geiranger - below, you can see cruise ships that look like toys. The cantilevered Skywalk extends over the drop above the fjord.

activities.text: Hellesylt-Geiranger cruise through UNESCO-listed Geirangerfjord. The Seven Sisters (De sju systre) cascade 410 metres in seven parallel streams down the fjord's north wall – opposite, the Suitor (Friaren) answers them from the other shore according to local legend. The journey takes around 1 hour 30 minutes depending on conditions.

Hike to the abandoned Skageflå farm, perched 250 metres above the fjord. Take the cruise out from Geiranger to be dropped off at the foot of the cliff, then climb the steep trail to the empty farm buildings. The view of the Seven Sisters from the same level offers a new perspective.

Kayak on Geirangerfjord at the foot of the waterfalls - the silence between the 1,700-metre walls is striking. Set out early morning when the cruise ships haven't yet arrived. Rental companies offer equipment and guides from Geiranger harbour.

Central Norway Road Trip: Ålesund, Geirangerfjord, Trollstigen & Trondheim

visits.text: The Struve Meridian Column at Fuglenes (UNESCO since 2005) is the northernmost point of a network of 265 triangulation stations stretching from Norway to the Black Sea—a 19th-century scientific project to measure the exact shape of the Earth. The walk to the monument offers a fine view over the harbor.

The Gjenreisningsmuseet tells how retreating Nazi forces razed Hammerfest in 1944—only the cemetery chapel remained standing. Audio testimonies from survivors, photographs, and period interior reconstructions show what it meant to rebuild everything from scratch. Allow at least an hour.
Hammerfest Church, rebuilt in 1961, has a triangular form inspired by traditional Sami tents—a subtle echo of the region's Sami past in a resolutely modern building.

The Isbjørnklubben (Royal Polar Bear Club) is a local institution founded in 1963—you can become a member by signing the register, which earns you a stamped diploma. A local curiosity worth seeing if you're passing through.

activities.text: Stroll along Hammerfest's waterfront: the harbor is lively, the multicolored 1950s houses tell the story of reconstruction, and you can watch seabirds from the pier in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Norway Road Trip: Tromsø, Alta & North Cape

visits.text: The E6 then E69 route crosses the Finnmark tundra—a treeless plateau where reindeer roam freely across the road. Plan to slow down: herds cross at all hours and they don't move aside quickly.
The North Cape Tunnel (Nordkapptunnelen) plunges 212m beneath the sea to reach the island of Magerøya—6.8km of undersea road tunnel. It's the gateway to Honningsvåg and North Cape.
Honningsvåg's colourful harbour, its roughly 2,800 inhabitants and its brightly coloured houses give a human scale to this far end of the continent.

The North Cape plateau stands 307 m above the Arctic Ocean: this is where the metal globe erected in 1978 rises, an iconic symbol of Europe's Far North. On a clear day, you look towards the North Pole with no intervening land except Svalbard, 2,100 km away. Allow for a return drive from Honningsvåg.

Nordkapphallen is largely carved into the rock: it houses a panoramic cinema showing the North Cape through the four seasons, an ecumenical chapel (Sankt Johanneskapell) and a permanent exhibition. Allow 1 hour to see everything - admission is charged. Also allow for a return drive from Honningsvåg.

Make the detour to Gjesvær to reach the cliffs of Gjesværstappan, one of Norway's largest seabird colonies - puffins, northern gannets and cormorants nest there in large numbers. From Honningsvåg, plan a return drive to Gjesvær, followed by a boat excursion to the cliffs. Boat excursions depart from the village.

activities.text: The road from Honningsvåg to North Cape crosses the island of Magerøya: a 34 km track winding among lakes, across tundra, and past sheep grazing freely along the roadside. In summer, not a tree blocks the horizon—the landscape is lunar and the sky immense.

From 13 May to 29 July, the sun does not set at the North Cape - it traces a complete circle around the horizon, bathing the cliff in permanent golden light. Stay until midnight to experience this spectacle from the cliff edge: few experiences compare. Allow for a return drive from Honningsvåg.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Norway Road Trip: Tromsø, Alta & North Cape
Northern Norway Road Trip: Tromsø, Alta & North Cape

visits.text: The ferry crossing from Lysebotn to Forsand travels the entire length of Lysefjord from its inner end—you'll see the walls of Kjerag and Preikestolen as you look along the fjord. Allow about 1 hour 30 minutes for the crossing, depending on the schedule. Check departures in advance; they're limited.
Stroll through Forsand village at the foot of Lysefjord - a few colorful houses, a quiet harbor, and views of the fjord walls from the quay. A good break after the previous days' efforts.

activities.text: Flørli houses the world's longest wooden staircase: 4,444 steps climbing through an elevation difference of 740 m along the old hydroelectric pipeline built between 1917 and 1921. The hamlet has no road access—you must take the ferry. At the top, Lake Ternevatnet and a view looking down over Lysefjord; descend via the Rallarstien to complete the loop.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: Posebyen, Kristiansand's historic quarter, survived the great fire of 1892 - the other neighborhoods burned, this one didn't. Founded in 1641 by King Christian IV, the city preserves its grid layout and single-story white wooden houses here. A peaceful atmosphere a stone's throw from the harbor.
Christiansholm fortress, completed in 1672 on an islet facing the harbor, was attacked only once, in 1807, by the British navy. Its walls are up to 5 m thick. Free entry, open April to October.
Fiskebrygga, Kristiansand's fish market, brings the waterfront to life with its boats and seafood stalls. A good vantage point for the harbor and the archipelago stretching out in front of the city.
Ravnedalen is a nature park right inside Kristiansand: ponds, waterfalls, and a small open-air stage amid the rocks. A quiet stroll 10 minutes' walk from the center, popular with locals.
Kristiansand Cathedral (Kristiansand domkirke), built in 1884 in neo-Gothic style, is Norway's third-largest church with 1,800 seats. You'll see its brick facade from the main square.

activities.text: Take a boat to explore Kristiansand's archipelago—small granite islands, colorful summer houses, and swimming in coves. In summer, regular services depart from the harbor for nearby islands.

The island of Bragdøya is accessible by boat from central Kristiansand in summer - coastal trails, rocky beaches and swimming in the calm waters of the archipelago. A perfect way to bring this road trip to a gentle close.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast
Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: The village of Bud, at the entrance to the Atlantic Ocean Road, was the busiest trading center between Bergen and Trondheim in the 16th-17th centuries. Allow for a round trip during the day from Kristiansund. Today, a few dozen red wooden houses face the open ocean - the contrast with the raging Hustadvika is striking in stormy weather.

The Atlantic Ocean Road (Atlanterhavsveien) links small islands over 8.3 km with 8 bridges facing the Norwegian Sea - built between 1983 and 1989 after weathering 12 violent storms during construction. Allow for a round trip during the day from Kristiansund. It was voted Norway's “construction of the century” in 2005. In bad weather, waves literally wash over the bridges.

The Storseisundet Bridge, 260 meters long, is the most photographed bridge on the road. Allow for a round trip during the day from Kristiansund. Its cantilevered curve creates an optical illusion from certain angles: the road appears to plunge straight into the ocean. Stop at the viewing area for the photo - you cannot get it from the car.

activities.text: Drive the Atlantic Ocean Road as a round trip from Kristiansund. Plan frequent stops at the four designated viewpoints along the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Norway Road Trip: Ålesund, Geirangerfjord, Trollstigen & Trondheim

visits.text: After the ferry crossing from Breivikeidet to Svensby, follow Route 91 along the Lyngenfjord: the Lyngen Alps rise above the fjord, with their rugged peaks and numerous glaciers. Stop at the viewpoints to enjoy the views of the mountains and their reflections in the fjord.

Lyngseidet is the main village on the Lyngen peninsula: a fjord on one side, glacier-carved rock faces on the other. This is where the ferry departs to cross the Lyngenfjord - allow approximately 40 minutes for the crossing.

activities.text: The hike to Blåisvatnet (Blue Lake) is the most popular in the Lyngen Alps: an 8 km round trip, 189 m of elevation gain, and relatively flat terrain apart from the final boulders before the lake. Its intense turquoise colour comes from meltwater from the Lenangsbreen glacier just above. Wear good footwear - the ground is stony throughout. From Lyngseidet, plan a return drive to the car park, followed by a hike to the lake.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Norway Road Trip: Tromsø, Alta & North Cape

visits.text: The road from Sirdal to Lysebotn crosses a mountain plateau where you might spot wild reindeer - keep your eyes on the roadside. The landscape changes dramatically as you descend toward the fjord.

Lysevegen: 27 dizzying switchbacks descend through an elevation difference of 640 m to reach the inner end of Lysefjord. Take your time on the bends—a few viewpoints let you grasp the scale of the descent.
Lysebotn has about ten permanent residents and serves as a base for BASE jumpers from around the world, drawn by Kjerag's walls. A place apart, at the end of the world, at the head of a fjord.

activities.text: Kjeragbolten is that 5 m³ boulder wedged between two cliffs 984 m above Lysefjord. The hike is 11 km round trip with 700 m elevation gain: metal chains on the steep sections help you climb, but the slabs can be slippery in wet weather. Allow 6 hours. Start early to avoid the queue at the boulder.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: Flekkefjord and its Dutch quarter (Hollenderbyen) feature rows of white facades reminiscent of the North Sea's trading towns - this architecture reveals the old trading ties with the Netherlands. An easy stop along the way. From Mandal, allow approximately 66 km and 1 hour of driving.

Sjøsanden beach in Mandal, 800 m long, is regularly voted Norway's best beach. It stretches within the Furulunden nature park, a 10-minute walk from the center - fine sand, calm water, pine forest backdrop.
Mandal's old town spreads out west of the harbor, with its winding lanes and white wooden houses. The town is the birthplace of sculptor Gustav Vigeland, whose works adorn Oslo's large park.

activities.text: Lindesnes fyr is Norway's first lighthouse - the first lantern was lit here in 1656, and the current cast-iron tower dates from 1915. You are at the southernmost point of mainland Norway, 2 518 km from the North Cape. From Mandal, allow approximately 39 km and 40 minutes of driving to the parking lot. The coastal trail from the parking lot is a 3 km round trip with a few rocky sections.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: Nusfjord is one of Norway's oldest fishing villages, with traces of human settlement dating back to 425 BC. In 1975, it was designated one of three UNESCO pilot projects in Norway for the preservation of traditional groups of wooden buildings. Today home to just 25 permanent residents, the village nonetheless welcomes 80,000 visitors per year. An entrance fee is charged in summer to contribute to site conservation.

Ramberg beach offers white sand with blue-green waters backed by mountains, the kind of panorama you'd expect more in the tropics. In July, you can swim here. Don't expect solitude: this is one of the most frequented beaches in the Lofoten in summer.

The Lofotr Viking Museum in Borg is approximately 37 km from Nusfjord, a 35-minute drive. It is built around the largest Viking longhouse ever discovered in Europe, unearthed in 1983 by a farmer ploughing his fields. The foundation measured 83 metres long and 9.5 metres wide, dated to around AD 500. The 1995 reconstruction lets you explore the interior, see replicas of Viking ships and watch craft demonstrations.

activities.text: The coastal trail from Nusfjord to Nesland runs past rocky coves and free-roaming sheep, with views over the fjord. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes for the 7 km round-trip, with no difficult elevation changes. The trail is poorly marked toward the end—download a GPS track before setting out.

places.name: Oslo

visits.text: Follow the Akerselva from Grünerløkka to the waterfalls and old mills - 9.8 km of trail threading through Oslo's industrial history. In 1856, the river's 20 cascades powered around twenty textile factories and flour mills. Walk it north to south: the view of the Opera House and fjord comes at the end.

The waterfront at Aker Brygge and Tjuvholmen shows you two faces of Oslo along the Oslofjord: former shipyards converted into restaurants and galleries on one side, the contemporary jetty at Tjuvholmen on the other. Walk out to the end of the pier for views across the fjord islands.

Climb onto the marble roof of Oslo Opera House (Operahuset) - it's free, open all the time, and the view over the fjord is the best in the city. The building, designed by Snøhetta and opened in 2008, is clad in Carrara marble and white granite. It won the Mies van der Rohe Prize in 2009. Pack slip-resistant shoes in winter: the roof gets slippery.
Oslo's Botanical Garden (Botanisk hage), in Tøyen, has existed since 1814 and houses one of Europe's largest collections of Nordic plants. Admission to the outdoor garden is free.

The Barcode Project, in the Bjørvika district, lines up a series of towers with striped facades designed by different architecture firms between 2005 and 2016. View them from the waterfront promenade - the barcode effect reads more clearly from a distance.

Climb up to the Damstredet and Telthusbakken neighbourhood, a ten-minute walk from the centre: you'll find painted wooden houses from the 18th and 19th centuries that survived Oslo's successive rebuildings. A striking contrast with the glass towers down by the water.

Sagene, Oslo's former industrial heartland, is now one of the city's most sought-after neighbourhoods. The name comes from Old Norwegian 'sager', meaning sawmills - the first date back to the 16th century. Wander past red-brick facades and former warehouses now converted into workshops and cafés.

The Norsk Folkemuseum at Bygdøy gathers over 150 historic buildings relocated from across Norway - it's one of Europe's largest open-air museums. The centrepiece is the Gol Stave Church, built around 1200 in the Hallingdal valley. In 1880, the municipality of Gol wanted to demolish it to build a new one. The Society for the Preservation of Ancient Monuments bought it, and King Oscar II funded its transfer to Bygdøy in 1884. On one of the nave pillars, a runic inscription reads: “Kiss me, for I struggle.” Allow 2 hours to tour the whole museum.

The former Viking Ship Museum (Vikingskipshuset) is currently closed. It is due to reopen in November 2027 as the Museum of the Viking Age (Vikingtidsmuseet). The new museum will notably display the famous Oseberg, Gokstad and Tune Viking ships, along with sledges, textiles and objects discovered in Viking burials. The 9th-century Oseberg ship was discovered in 1904 in a burial mound near Tønsberg.

The Holmenkollen Ski Museum is the world's oldest ski museum - it opened in 1923 and traces 4,000 years of skiing history, from Stone Age rock carvings to the gear from Fridtjof Nansen and Roald Amundsen's polar expeditions. The facade was completely renovated by Snøhetta in 2023. The building is carved into the mountain, beneath the ski jump.

From the viewing platform atop Holmenkollbakken - a ski jump built in 1892 and rebuilt for the 1952 Oslo Olympics - you get the panoramic view of the city and Oslofjord that every guidebook describes. It deserves its reputation. Take the lift, then climb 114 steps to the top. Allow 30 to 40 minutes to explore the summit. Avoid competition days if you want the terrace to yourself.

On the RV7, the crossing of Hardangervidda gives you 67 km of lunar landscape - northern Europe's largest high-altitude plateau, at 1,100-1,200 metres. Lake after lake, open heath and infinite horizons. It's also one of the few places in Europe where wild reindeer migrate freely: several thousand animals cross the plateau with the seasons.
In Hol, stop to see Hol Gamle Kyrkje (Hol's old church). A brief stop of 15-20 minutes is enough to see the exterior and the historic cemetery.

activities.text: Photo walk through Sentrum: the colourful facades and heritage buildings of the historic centre are particularly photogenic late in the day when low-angle light cuts through the narrow streets. Head from City Hall towards Parliament for an hour of urban wandering.

Return ferry trip from Aker Brygge to Bygdøy - approximately 10 minutes across the Oslofjord. It is the most enjoyable way to reach the Bygdøy peninsula and its museums, with lovely views of the fjord's islands.

Holmenkollen hosts annual biathlon and ski jumping competitions at the national arena - dates vary according to the FIS and IBU calendars. When no competitions are taking place, the cross-country ski trails of Nordmarka start just behind the jump. Reach Holmenkollen by metro (line 1, Holmenkollen station, 25 minutes from the centre).

Return by car from Ulvik to Oslo via the RV7 and the E16: allow approximately 5 hours 5 minutes of driving, excluding breaks. Pass through Geilo to refuel if needed. Check conditions on vegvesen.no in autumn and spring: the RV7 can close during snowstorms on the plateau.

visits.text: Reine is nestled between sharp peaks and the blue-green waters of the Reinefjorden—the most reproduced postcard image of the Lofoten. The light here is spectacular at any hour, but especially at dusk. Park at the harbor and explore the lanes around the rorbu on foot.

The Fredvang bridges span several small islands between Flakstad and Moskenesøy, with views down over the Selfjorden. Plan for the return drive from Reine. Stop by the roadside for a photo: the view of the arched bridges with the mountains behind them is one of the most photographed in the Lofoten Islands.

The hamlet of Hamnøy, 5 minutes from Reine, is home to the most photographed red rorbu in the Lofoten, facing the Reinefjorden and sheer rock walls. This is the most accessible sunset and midnight sun spot from Reine. Plan to be here early in the morning or late in the evening to avoid groups of photographers.

Å i Lofoten is the last village at the end of the E10 road. Its name is a single letter meaning “river” in Old Norse. This was the end of the road at the edge of the world before modern tunnels. The Fishing Village Museum (Norsk Fiskeværsmuseum), founded in 1988, brings together several period buildings including a cod liver oil factory still in working order and an 1878 bakery. In summer, cinnamon rolls fresh from the stone oven await you here.

The Stockfish Museum (Lofoten Tørrfiskmuseum), set in a former fish landing hall, explains the entire cod-drying process—from fishing in January to export to Italy. Lofoten stockfish is now a protected designation at the European level, just like Roquefort. If you've seen cod-drying racks all along the route, this is where you'll understand why.

Reine is often described as Norway's most beautiful village—hard to dispute when you arrive by road and the red cabins on stilts suddenly appear facing the peaks plunging into Reinefjord. Reine's rorbuer, painted red, were once the lodgings of fishermen who came from the mainland to fish for cod from January to April. Many have been converted into accommodations—book well in advance.

A few kilometres away, the village of Å (pronounced “Ô”) marks the end of the road. This remote spot can be explored like an open-air museum: a boathouse, a cod-liver oil factory, a forge, a former post office and rorbuer. The Norwegian Fishing Village Museum traces the history of cod fishing in 7 buildings. Do not miss Hamnøy: the red cabins seen from the bridge may be the best-known photograph of the Lofoten Islands.

Kvalvika beach is one of the most beautiful in the Lofoten Islands: a white-sand cove ringed by 400-metre peaks that plunge into the Arctic. From Reine, plan a day trip by car to the Fredvang parking area and back. You then reach the beach on foot, with a 1-hour walk to the beach along a marked trail. Bring waterproof footwear. Along the way, the Fredvang bridges - two suspension bridges over a strait between three islands - are among the most popular photo spots in the Lofoten Islands.

In the late afternoon, take the detour to Nusfjord, approximately 41 km from Reine, a 40-minute drive. It is one of the best-preserved fishing villages in the Lofoten Islands, tucked away at the head of a fjord. There is an admission fee, but it gives you access to a village that seems straight out of the 1900s. Take the path that climbs at the entrance for a panoramic view before heading down to stroll along the pier.

activities.text: Reinebringen is the most famous hike in the Lofoten, with 1,978 stone steps built by Nepalese Sherpas between 2016 and 2021 to stabilize the trail. The summit reaches 448 meters, with a view down over Reine, Hamnøy, and the Reinefjorden. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours round-trip. Avoid it in wet weather—the steps become slippery and the view disappears. In July, start before 8 a.m. to avoid lines on the trail.

The hike to the hidden beach of Kvalvika from Fredvang crosses moorland and low ridges with views of the Selfjord. From Reine, plan a return drive to the trailhead near Fredvang, then continue on foot. The beach, accessible only on foot, remains wild and little visited outside July. Allow 3 hours for the 6 km round trip.

Sea kayaking between the small islands of the Reinefjorden is an ideal evening activity - from late May to mid-July, you paddle under the midnight sun between rock faces plunging straight into the water. Operators offer rentals and guided trips departing from Reine.

The Reinebringen hike (448 m) is the most famous in the Lofoten. The ascent is on a staircase of 1,600 stone steps laid in 2019 by Nepalese workers accustomed to Himalayan trails. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours for the ascent. At the summit, the view down over the Reinefjord, Kjerkfjord and Vorfjord with the red cabins below is the most photographed panorama in the Lofoten. Leave early—the parking lot fills up quickly in season.

Spend the morning on Rambergstranda or Skagsanden beach, two white-sand beaches easily accessible from the road. From Reine, plan a day trip by car to these beaches and back. In fine weather, the reflection of the mountains in the water is striking. The water is cold, but some people swim here in summer.

visits.text: The Senja National Scenic Route (Nasjonal turistveg Senja) connects Gryllefjord in the west to Botnhamn in the north. This is the route Norwegians themselves call the most beautiful in the national network. Take your time: every bend reveals cliffs 700 to 800 meters tall plunging straight into the Atlantic, hidden coves, and isolated villages.

Husøy is an active fishing village perched on its own islet in the Øyfjorden, connected to Senja by a 300-meter causeway. The colorful houses are anchored with cables to the ground to withstand storms. Local legend has it that the custom of the midday siesta, still practiced here, was introduced by Spanish Armada sailors shipwrecked on these shores in 1588.

The Bergsbotn viewing platform is cantilevered over the Bergsfjorden and is easily reached from the road. It frames the fjord and ridges like a painting. Be wary of the road leading up to it—it's very narrow, with motorhomes coming the other way.

From Tungeneset beach, a Siberian larch boardwalk crosses the rocks toward a promontory facing the Okshornan—the Devil's Teeth, three granite peaks rising from the ocean. Pools on the rocks reflect the summits in calm weather: bring a tripod for your photos. It's also one of the island's best spots for northern lights at night.

Ersfjordstranda beach is a strip of white sand framed by steep mountains—the kind of landscape you don't expect at this latitude. Don't miss the famous golden cabin: the gold-colored stainless steel public toilet, which has become an attraction in its own right on the island.

activities.text: Ferry crossing from Tromsø to Senja via the Brensholmen–Botnhamn route—about a 45-minute link that drops you directly at the start of the scenic route. The drive from Tromsø to Brensholmen takes about 1 hour. Arrive early at Botnhamn to start the scenic route in morning light.

visits.text: Step into Gamle Stavanger, Norway's best-preserved old quarter: 173 white wooden houses from the 18th and 19th centuries, flower-filled facades, and cobbled lanes. Allow a good hour to explore - this is a living residential neighborhood, not a frozen museum piece.

Stavanger Cathedral (Stavanger domkirke), founded around 1125, is Norway's oldest cathedral still in active use. The original Romanesque nave contrasts with the Gothic choir rebuilt after the 1272 fire—a fine example of architecture from two periods.

Øvre Holmegate, nicknamed the "street of colors" (Fargegaten), brings together brightly painted facades and a handful of trendy cafes. A striking contrast to the white houses of Gamle Stavanger, just a stone's throw away.

The Norwegian Petroleum Museum traces the oil saga from the discovery of the first North Sea fields in the 1960s. The building itself, opened in 1999, resembles an oil platform set in the harbor—you can't miss it.
The Norwegian Canning Museum occupies a converted sardine factory: you'll see cans being smoked on-site and understand how this industry built the city before oil took over. A packed half-hour.
The Stavanger Museum houses collections of natural history and regional archaeology, including Viking Age artifacts. Handy for preparing for tomorrow's hike with some regional context.

From the boat, you'll see Preikestolen from a completely different angle - the platform looks tiny against the 600 m of sheer wall. Many say it's even more impressive seen from below than from the summit.
Hengjanefossen waterfall plunges directly into the fjord from the cliffs: visible from the boat deck, it alone illustrates the immensity of Lysefjord.
Fantahålå cave (Vagabond's Cave) extends into the cliffs halfway up—the cruise guide will tell you when to look for it from the deck.

activities.text: Stroll from Vågen harbor to the fish market (Fisketorget): fresh shrimp, smoked salmon, and the maritime atmosphere of Stavanger's waterfront. The trick here is to arrive early for the best shrimp.

The Preikestolen hike is one of Norway's most famous: an 8 km round trip with 500 m of elevation gain, reaching a 25x25 m platform suspended 604 m above the Lysefjord. Set off before 7 a.m. - more than 300 000 hikers visit each year, and the daytime crowds can be overwhelming. From Stavanger, drive to the parking lot at Preikestolen fjellstue, where the hike starts.

The Lysefjord cruise from Stavanger travels the 42 km length of the fjord between cliffs that plunge from heights of up to 1,000 m. Allow 3 hours round trip. Book ahead in high season—boats depart in the morning from Stavanger harbor.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast
Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast
Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: Svolvær harbor is packed with rorbu—the iconic red wooden fishermen's cabins on stilts of the Lofoten. Walk out onto the Svinøya quay to see the cod-drying racks lined up on the rocks and the statue of the Fisherman's Wife (Fiskerkona). This is the natural crossroads of the archipelago before plunging south.

The Gunnar Berg Gallery at Svinøya displays the work of the painter born in Svolvær in 1863. His most famous painting depicts the Battle of Trollfjord in 1890—a revolt by small-scale fishermen in rowboats against industrial steamships blocking the entrance to the fjord with their nets. This painting became a national political symbol and contributed to the passage of the Lofoten fishing law.

Henningsvær is a fishing village of 510 inhabitants spread across several small islands linked by bridges, approximately 24 km from Svolvær, a 25-minute drive. Its football pitch is more famous than the village itself: carved into the rock since 1927, surrounded by sea on all sides and sheer peaks, it is the most photographed amateur stadium in the world. Climb the rock south of the pitch for the best view.

The KaviarFactory in Henningsvær is a former cod roe factory converted into an international contemporary art gallery. Allow approximately 24 km from Svolvær, a 25-minute drive. It has become one of Norway's most unexpected art venues. Go inside even if contemporary art is not your priority: the industrial building on the waterfront is worth a look.
The white-sand beach of Rørvikstranda has clear waters. You can swim there in July - the water reaches 15 to 17°C.

Kabelvåg Church (Vågan kirke), built in 1898, is nicknamed the Lofoten Cathedral—with 1,200 seats, it's the largest wooden church in northern Norway. It was built to accommodate the thousands of seasonal fishermen who converged on Kabelvåg in winter. Visit in the early morning: it's often open and not crowded.

The Lofoten Aquarium (Lofotakvariet) in Kabelvåg presents local marine wildlife in outdoor and indoor tanks: otters, seals and fish from Arctic fjords. It is a good option for families or when the weather rules out hiking.

Kabelvåg is historically the first commercial center of the Lofoten, founded in the 12th century by King Øystein Magnusson who built a shelter for fishermen there—making it one of the first towns in northern Norway. Stroll through the old center around the harbor: the 19th-century wooden houses are well preserved.

Welcome to the Lofoten. The Narvik–Svolvær route via the E10 (3–4 hours) is an experience in itself: it runs along fjords, passes through tunnels carved into rock and crosses suspension bridges between islands. Svolvær, the de facto capital of the Lofoten with 5,000 inhabitants, lives to the rhythm of its harbor. Head down to the quays: fishing boats, cod drying racks, rorbuer on stilts reflecting in the water. Skrei fishing (Arctic cod) remains the archipelago's engine—between January and April, Svolvær sees the world's largest cod catches.

Look up from the harbor: the Svolværgeita dominates the city from the flank of Mount Fløyfjellet. These two 150-meter rock pinnacles, nicknamed “the Svolvær Goat,” are the city's emblem. Climbers from around the world come to scale them. For the view without ropes, climb to Fløya (590 m, 2 hours from the center)—a guaranteed 360° panorama over the archipelago.

Step inside the Gunnar Berg Gallery, dedicated to the painter born here in 1863. His canvases capture the light of the Lofoten in the 19th century—stormy skies, reflections on water, fishermen's silhouettes. A way to understand these landscapes beyond photographs.

activities.text: The mini-cruise into Trollfjorden is the must-do excursion from Svolvær. This arm of the sea measures only 2.5 km long by 100 meters wide at the entrance, framed by walls exceeding 1,000 meters—Trolltindan peaks at 1,084 m. Operators offer daily departures in silent electric boats or fast RIBs. Book an early-morning departure for the best light on the cliffs.

The Festvågtind hike above Henningsvær offers a bird's-eye view of the village's small islands and their bridges. From Svolvær, plan a return drive to the trailhead near Henningsvær, then continue on foot. The uphill trail is approximately 5 km round trip with 490 metres of elevation gain. Allow 3 hours for an average walker. The route to the summit is not marked throughout - hiking boots are essential; avoid it in wet weather.

The Fløya hike above Svolvær is an accessible alternative to climbing Svolværgeita (the two iconic rock horns reserved for experienced climbers). The round-trip hike to Fløya takes 2 hours over 4 km and offers a view over the harbor, islets, and surrounding mountains. Start early in the morning to enjoy the panorama before the afternoon clouds.

Take a speedboat excursion to Trollfjord, a 2 km fjord arm squeezed between vertical granite walls - so narrow that large boats can barely maneuver there. This is also where white-tailed eagles, with their wingspan of over 2 meters, dive to catch fish. Operators offer this outing departing from the harbor.

visits.text: Ishavskatedralen, designed by architect Jan Inge Hovig, was inaugurated on November 19, 1965. Its 11 aluminum-clad concrete panels on each side of the roof create the triangular silhouette visible from both the bridge and the airport. Inside, don't miss Victor Sparre's glass mosaic (1972) on the east side—it depicts the hand of God radiating three beams of light. Midnight sun concerts are held here in summer: check the program before your visit.

Tromsø's waterfront stretches along the Skansen district, where the old wooden harbor warehouses date back in some cases to the 1830s. This was the base from which shipowners financed Arctic expeditions in the 19th century—Tromsø was known as the Gateway to the Arctic. Walk here in the evening: the low-angle light on the colorful facades is particularly beautiful.

The Polar Museum (Polarmuseet) is housed in an 1830 customs warehouse and opened in 1978 on the exact 50th anniversary of Roald Amundsen's last departure from Tromsø. Inside you'll encounter his authentic equipment, a reconstructed Svalbard trapper's hut, and the story of Henry Rudi—a hunter who killed 713 polar bears over 27 winters and was a national hero of his era. Arrive in the morning: the museum is small and fills up quickly in the afternoons.

The Arctic-Alpine Botanical Garden is the world's northernmost botanical garden, open since 1994 on the university campus, with free admission at all hours. Its 25 collections bring together Arctic and alpine plants from every continent, from Tibet to Patagonia. The Himalayan blue poppy (Meconopsis) is its signature plant. Note that it closes when covered in snow in winter.

The Arctic University Museum of Norway (Norges arktiske universitetsmuseum) brings together collections on Sami culture, Arctic wildlife, and High North geology. You'll find presentations on the lives of Sami reindeer herders and their seasonal migrations—a valuable counterpoint before entering the landscapes ahead. Allow 1 hour 15 minutes and grab a map at the entrance: signage is primarily in Norwegian.

The Skansen district contains Tromsø's best-preserved wooden houses, painted in white, yellow, and red according to local tradition. This was the old residential heart of the city, established in the late 18th century. Take a walking tour in the afternoon: the streets are quiet, the facades photogenic.

Tromsø Cathedral (Tromsø Domkirke), built in wood in 1861, is one of Norway's largest wooden cathedrals. It stands out with its understated neo-Gothic style against the waterfront architecture. If you're here on a Sunday morning, the service is open to visitors.

Bodø→Tromsø flight (around 1 hour). Tromsø: an island connected to the mainland by a one-kilometer bridge, surrounded by fjords and mountains 350 km north of the Arctic Circle. With 77,000 inhabitants, it's Norway's eighth largest city, nicknamed the “Paris of the North”—a nickname from the 19th century, when upper-class women had their dresses imported directly from Paris and nightlife was surprisingly lively for such a northern city. Start with the Arctic Cathedral (Ishavskatedralen), built in 1964–1965 by architect Jan Inge Hovig: its triangular silhouette symbolizes icebergs, the long darkness and the northern lights. The eastern stained glass window—140 m² of glass—is one of Europe's largest.

The Polar Museum (Polarmuseet) occupies a former customs warehouse dating from 1833, listed as a national heritage site since 2000. It traces whaling, sealing, and the great polar expeditions. Roald Amundsen—the first man to reach the South Pole in 1911—has an entire room devoted to him, as does Fridtjof Nansen. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

At the end of the day, stroll through Tromsø's old town: the colorful wooden houses from the 19th and 20th centuries are among the best preserved in Northern Norway. The wooden church in the center (Tromsø Domkirke, 1861) is Norway's only wooden Lutheran cathedral.

Start with the Fjellheisen cable car, in service since 1961. In four minutes, it takes you up to 420 meters on Mount Storsteinen. The panorama takes in the city on its island, the one-kilometer bridge, the fjords and mountains on the horizon. In winter, it's one of Tromsø's best spots to observe the auroras. In summer, it's the starting point for hikers heading to Tromsdalstinden (1,238 m).

Stop by Mack Brewery, founded in 1877 by Ludwig Markus Mack, son of a German immigrant. Mack long remained the world's northernmost brewery. Its historic pub, Ølhallen, open since 1928, is Tromsø's oldest brewery-bar. It's the perfect spot for an Arctic beer facing the old docks.
A detour through Polaria, the Arctic aquarium whose building evokes white concrete dominoes toppled by a wave. Inside, bearded seals, Arctic fish and an exhibition on phenomena of the Far North.

activities.text: The Fjellheisen cable car opened on February 22, 1961, and carries passengers in 4 minutes up to the Storsteinen plateau at 421 meters. From there, the view sweeps across the entire city on its island and the Lyngen Alps in the distance. In winter, this is one of Tromsø's best spots for northern lights. Book ahead in high season—the cabins hold only 28 people.

Head out on a boat excursion into the Kvaløysundet to observe white-tailed eagles—the fjords around Tromsø are home to one of Europe's densest populations. These birds, with wingspans that can exceed 2.4 meters, dive for fish at the surface. Operators offer 2-hour trips departing from the harbor; book ahead in high season.

In the dark season (September–March), a nighttime northern lights excursion from Tromsø is essential. Operators offer outings by minibus or boat to the surrounding fjords. Tromsø is one of Europe's best bases for this: the sky is statistically clear more often than in other places at comparable latitudes.

If you have a car, head out to the island of Kvaløya for wild fjords less than an hour away. Local hikers go there all year round. In the evening, prepare for your flight back to Stockholm the following day.

places.name: Trondheim

visits.text: Nidaros Cathedral (Nidarosdomen) is the world's northernmost Gothic cathedral. Construction began in 1070 on the tomb of Saint Olav - a Viking king who died at Stiklestad in 1030 and was canonised a year later. His silver shrine was melted down for coins at the 1537 Reformation and his remains buried in a secret location within the cathedral that no one has found since.

The Archbishop's Palace (Erkebispegården), right next to the cathedral, is Scandinavia's oldest secular building still standing. It houses the Norwegian crown jewels and an archaeological exhibition on medieval Trondheim.

Bakklandet is Trondheim's most photogenic quarter - its colourful wooden houses and cobbled streets date from the 1600s. In 1965, the city council wanted to demolish the district for a four-lane highway; activists reclaimed the empty houses in 1971 and painted the façades to save them. Cross the Old Bridge (Gamle Bybro, 1681) to reach it from the centre.

The wooden storehouses on stilts (Bryggen) lining the Nidelva are Trondheim's equivalent of Bergen's Bryggen - built partly into the river to allow boats to moor directly. The view from the Old Bridge is Trondheim's postcard shot.

Kristiansten Fortress (1681), built after the great fire that devastated Trondheim the same year, dominates the town from its hilltop. From here you have the best view of the Nidelva storehouses, the cathedral and the distant fjord. Entry is free.

Ringve Museum, the national museum of music, occupies an 18th-century manor surrounded by botanical gardens. The collection of historical instruments is displayed in the original rooms - guides play live during the tour.

Munkholmen island, accessible in 10 minutes by boat from the harbour, has served variously as an execution site, Benedictine monastery (11th century), prison (17th century) and fortress. In summer, Trondheim locals swim from the beach there.

Trøndelag Folk Museum (Trøndelag Folkemuseum) at Sverresborg brings together historic farms and buildings in an open-air setting on the hills above Trondheim. The medieval Sverresborg fortress stands prominently at the centre of the site.

Trampe, the world's only bicycle lift, has stood on the Brubakken slope in Bakklandet since 1993. You place your foot on the pedal platform, the mechanism pushes – and you ascend the steep hill effortlessly. Available during the summer season.

activities.text: Wander through Bakklandet's lanes – the district's crooked houses are home to a concentration of independent cafés, bookshops and craft boutiques. Don't miss Trampe, the world's first bicycle lift, installed on the Brubakken slope in 1993.

The Ladestien coastal path follows 14 km of coastline north of Trondheim with views over Trondheimsfjord. You can walk part of it from Nedre Elvehavn - allow 2 to 3 hours for a one-way stretch to Lade and return by bus.

At the Sverresborg museum in Trondheim, follow the paths between the farms and historic buildings of Trøndelag. Observe the architecture of the houses, then climb to the remains of the medieval fortress to see the city and the fjord. This walk through the open-air museum offers a glimpse of the region's traditional ways of life.

visits.text: Steinsdalsfossen waterfall, 2 km from Norheimsund, is one of Norway's most visited for a simple reason: you can walk behind it and stay dry. A paved path follows the riverbank, climbs behind the 46-metre curtain of water and comes out on the cliff side. Kaiser Wilhelm II came here every summer for 25 years - until 1914; snowmelt flow peaks in May-June. Plan a same-day round trip from Ulvik.

The Hardanger suspension bridge (Hardangerbrua), opened in 2013, spans Hardangerfjord for 1,380 metres - one of the world's longest suspension bridges. It replaced a ferry service that connected Bruravik and Brimnes for decades. Stop at one of the panoramic viewpoints to see it in its entirety from the shore.

Ulvik, a village of a few hundred inhabitants at the head of Ulvikafjord, is nicknamed 'Norway's orchard'. The slopes around the fjord are covered with thousands of apple, pear and cherry trees - English Cistercian monks introduced fruit cultivation here in the 13th century. In May, the blossoming orchards transform the village into an Impressionist painting. Stroll along the waterfront and fjord shore.

The Ulvik Fruit and Cider Route is the only one of its kind in Norway: three family farms welcome you for cider and apple juice tastings. Hardanger cider has been awarded Protected Geographical Indication status - Norway's equivalent of an AOC. In autumn, harvests are at their peak.

The trails above Ulvik offer views down over Ulvikafjord and Osafjord - two quiet arms of Hardangerfjord encircled by orchards and birch forests. Marked local trails start directly from the village. Pack hiking shoes: some sections are on a slope and can be slippery in wet weather.

Vøringsfossen waterfall, 20 km from Eidfjord, is Norway's most famous: 163 metres of free fall from the Hardangervidda plateau into the Måbødalen valley. In 1880, a hotel was built right on the edge - all the materials were carried up on horseback from Eidfjord. A 47-metre bridge opened in 2020, with 99 steps above the gorge, offers a dizzying view of the waterfall. For access by car from Ulvik, allow approximately 52 km and a 50-minute drive.

activities.text: Drive from Bergen to Ulvik via Norheimsund and Hardangerfjord: allow 2 hours 30 minutes. The scenic Alvikvegen road along the fjord is worth the detour - the road hugs the water a few metres up with constant views over the green waters of Hardangerfjord and the snow-capped peaks in the background.

Scenic loop from Ulvik to Eidfjord and back via RV7 - allow half a day. The section of road that descends through the hairpin tunnels of Måbødalen valley is spectacular: the transition from lunar plateau at 1,250 m to green valley to fjord happens in a few kilometres.

visits.text: Henningsvær, nicknamed the “Venice of the Lofoten,” spreads across several small islands connected by bridges—on Google Maps, you can clearly see the shape of the miniature archipelago. Park at the entrance and explore on foot: the streets are too narrow for cars. The harbor and its old converted fishing warehouses are listed as cultural heritage sites in Norway. Cod fishing remains the main activity—in February–March, the cod season transforms the quays into a scene of continuous work.

Henningsvær's soccer field is probably the most photographed in the world: built on a rocky islet between two arms of the sea, without stands—spectators bring their own chairs. The local club uses it for amateur matches, and the site also hosts concerts and festivals.

The KaviarFactory is one of the most unexpected cultural surprises in Northern Norway. Opened in 2013 in a former 1950s caviar factory converted into 500 m² of exhibition space, it presents internationally renowned artists—Ai Weiwei, Marina Abramovic, Yoko Ono have all exhibited here. A short walk away, Galleri Lofoten displays the largest collection of paintings from the “golden age of North Norwegian art” (1870–1930). Two museums of international standing in a village of 500 inhabitants.

activities.text: For a short but striking hike, climb Festvågtind (541 m). The ascent is difficult and short, but the 360° view over Henningsvær, the archipelago and the open sea is one of the most beautiful in the eastern Lofoten. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes round trip. Operators also offer sea kayaking among the islets around the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Scandinavia Road Trip: Stockholm to the Lofoten Islands

visits.text: The Abisko–Narvik road (85 km, 1 hour 15 minutes) crosses the Norwegian border at Riksgränsen and descends toward the fjords. In Narvik, begin at the War Museum (Narviksenteret). The Battle of Narvik from April 9 to June 8, 1940, lasted 62 days and cost 8,500 lives. It was at Narvik that Allied forces—British, French, Polish and Norwegian—won their very first land victory against Nazi Germany. The museum recounts these 62 days battle by battle, through photos, films and recorded eyewitness accounts. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

Narvik's harbor deserves a stroll: it's why the battle took place. Narvik was the export port for iron ore from Kiruna (Sweden) - an ice-free port year-round, connected to the Swedish mines by the Ofotbanen, the railway line built in 1902. Hitler needed this ore for his war industry: 90% of Swedish iron passed through Narvik in winter. The city still lives to the rhythm of this rail traffic.

activities.text: Take the cable car up Narvikfjellet for a panoramic view of the city, Ofotfjord and mountains from 656 meters. In summer under the midnight sun, the panorama is striking; in winter, it's one of the best vantage points for northern lights away from city lights.
